title: The great encyclopedia
hookLine: Kahn Singh Nabha compiled the Mahan Kosh, a vast Sikh encyclopedia

lines: AN OLD WORD IN A HYMN.
cards: A word in a hymn stops a reader cold. It's old. It might be Persian, or Sanskrit, or a Punjabi word nobody in the village uses anymore.
The granthi doesn't know it. The uncle who knows everything doesn't know it either. Where do you go?
For Sikh readers in the time of the reform movement, the answer was slowly being built, one entry at a time, by a scholar from the princely state of Nabha: a book that could say what a word means.

teach.b: First, the name. Kahn Singh's book is called the Mahan Kosh. Mahan means great.
Kosh means a store, a treasury, and in Punjabi it's the word for a dictionary. Its full title calls it a sea of jewels of the Guru's word. Second, what's inside.
It gathers the words of the Guru Granth Sahib and the other Sikh writings, and alongside them people, places, gurdwaras, ragas, weapons, plants and customs.
Look up a name from the Gurus' lives and you find who that person was. Look up a raga and you find the musical setting. Look up an ordinary word and you may find how it's used in a hymn.

Tradition says Kahn Singh spent many years on it, checking each entry against the texts. On a page of it today, the care shows: short entries, cross-references, a scholar who wanted readers to find their own way.

Fourth, why it matters. Sikhs often point out that the Gurus sang in the speech of their own listeners, not in a scholars' language. Guru Nanak's hymns speak of the word, the shabad, as what carries a person across.

teach.h: CLEARING THE FOG FROM A HYMN.
teach.b: But words drift, and a hymn that was plain to its first listeners can turn foggy.

A book like the Mahan Kosh clears the fog, so the hymn can speak plainly again. Sikh readers and translators still reach for it. The reformers of the Singh Sabha years wanted Sikhs to know who they were.
Kahn Singh's answer was practical: know your own words.

how: Sikh readers, students and translators use Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's Mahan Kosh to look up words, names and places from the Guru Granth Sahib and other Sikh writings, in print and in digital editions.

games.q: you're a reformer who wants Sikhs to know their own tradition. hymns are full of words that have grown unfamiliar. what do you build?
o: a new set of hymns in modern words.
a great treasury that explains the old words and names.
nothing; the meaning will come back on its own.
games.why: Kahn Singh built the Mahan Kosh: it leaves the hymns as they are and helps the reader understand them.

practice: Bring to mind a word you've heard in a prayer, a song, a hymn or a sermon and never quite understood, in any tradition, any language: Waheguru, Amen, grace, something your grandmother said.
Hold it gently, and notice whether you've been living with a guess. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Mahan Kosh, the great treasury of words, compiled by Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha so readers could find what the Guru's words mean. Today's word.
